concepts.title: Helm Charts and Templating
concepts.description: Helm packages a set of related Kubernetes manifests into a single, versioned, parameterized chart. Go templating over a values.yaml file lets one chart definition render differently for dev, staging, and production, replacing what would otherwise be dozens of hand-maintained, drifting near-duplicate YAML files.
learningObjectives: Explain the specific maintenance problems that emerge when raw YAML manifests are hand-duplicated across multiple services and environments.
Describe a Helm chart's directory structure and the role of Chart.yaml, values.yaml, and the templates/ directory.
Use Go template syntax ({{ .Values.x }}, {{ .Release.Name }}, conditionals, ranges, pipelines) to parameterize a manifest.
Explain how values.yaml defaults are overridden at install/upgrade time via -f and --set, and the precedence order between them.
Use helm template and helm lint to inspect a chart's fully rendered output before it ever reaches the cluster.
Predict and fix a common templating bug caused by multi-line values breaking YAML indentation when rendered.

sections.heading: Why Raw YAML Stops Scaling
sections.body:
A single Deployment-plus-Service pair is easy to hand-write and hand-edit. The trouble multiplies: with N services each running in M environments (dev, staging, prod, maybe a per-developer sandbox), you maintain close to N times M near-duplicate YAML files that differ in a handful of values: an image tag, a replica count, a resource limit, an environment variable pointing at a different database host. Plain YAML has no mechanism to say 'these 40 files are really one template with different parameters'; they're 40 independent files that happen to look similar today.

The failure mode is drift: someone bumps the memory limit in the production Deployment during an incident and forgets staging; a new label gets added to 12 of 20 copies because the other 8 were edited by someone who didn't know to add it. There's also no single version number for 'this bundle of manifests, as deployed to production last Tuesday.' To see what changed between two deploys you diff raw files by hand, and to roll back you revert each file manually and hope you didn't miss one. Helm's answer is to stop treating each environment's manifests as independent files and treat them as one parameterized template rendered differently per environment, with the parameter values captured and versioned as a first-class artifact.

sections.heading: Anatomy of a Chart
sections.body:
A Helm chart is a directory with a fixed, conventional structure:

```text
my-app/
├── Chart.yaml          # chart metadata: name, version, appVersion
├── values.yaml         # default configuration values
├── charts/             # bundled sub-charts (dependencies), if any
└── templates/
    ├── deployment.yaml  # Go-template-annotated Kubernetes manifests
    ├── service.yaml
    ├── _helpers.tpl     # reusable named template snippets
    └── NOTES.txt        # post-install usage text shown to the user
```

`Chart.yaml` carries the chart's identity: its `name`, its own semantic `version` (how the chart's packaging has changed), and separately `appVersion` (the version of the application it deploys). These are independent, since you can ship a packaging fix without the application changing, or vice versa. `values.yaml` holds the chart author's defaults for every parameter the templates reference. Dependencies on other charts are declared in `Chart.yaml` and fetched into `charts/` with `helm dependency update`. Everything under `templates/` is not valid Kubernetes YAML by itself: it's Go template *source*, with `{{ }}` placeholders that become real YAML only when Helm renders them with actual values. `_helpers.tpl` holds reusable snippets (a standard label block, a computed name, anything referenced from several templates via `{{ include "my-app.labels" . }}`) so you don't repeat the same boilerplate in every file.

sections.heading: Templating with Go Templates: Values, Objects, and Control Flow
sections.body:
Inside a template file, `{{ .Values.image.tag }}` reaches into the merged values data (covered in the next section) and substitutes whatever `image.tag` resolves to. A few other built-in objects sit alongside `.Values`: `.Release.Name` and `.Release.Namespace` (the release being installed, covered in the next concept), and `.Chart.Name`/`.Chart.Version` (metadata from Chart.yaml).

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-{{ .Chart.Name }}
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount | default 1 }}
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
          {{- if .Values.resources }}
          resources:
            {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }}
          {{- end }}
```

`| default 1` is a **pipeline**: it feeds `.Values.replicaCount` into the `default` function, which substitutes `1` if the value is empty or unset, a fallback independent of whatever's in `values.yaml`. `{{- if .Values.resources }} ... {{- end }}` is a conditional block that emits the enclosed YAML only if `resources` is set, so an unset value doesn't leave behind a `resources:` key rendered as `null` or an empty block. `{{- range .Values.env }} ... {{- end }}` (not shown above) is the looping construct, used for list-shaped values such as a variable number of environment variables. The leading `{{-` (and a trailing `-}}`, in place of plain `{{`/`}}`) are whitespace-trim markers: they strip the newline and indentation immediately before or after the tag, which keeps the output from accumulating stray blank lines around every conditional or loop. Together with `nindent`, which the Multi-Line Indentation Trap section below covers, that whitespace control decides where each generated block starts on the page, and so whether the rendered file is the YAML you meant. For a value that must be supplied, the `required` function turns a silent blank into a render-time error: `{{ required "image.tag is required" .Values.image.tag }}`.

sections.heading: Overriding Defaults: values.yaml Precedence
sections.body:
`values.yaml` inside the chart supplies the chart author's defaults, but almost nobody deploys a chart with only those defaults in every environment. Helm layers values from multiple sources, and the precedence order, highest wins, is: `--set` flags on the command line, then `-f`/`--values` files in the order given (later files override earlier ones), then the chart's own bundled `values.yaml` as the final fallback.

```bash
helm install web ./my-app \
  -f values-prod.yaml \
  --set replicaCount=5 \
  --set image.tag=2.3.1
```

Merging is a **deep merge** on maps, not a wholesale replacement: if the chart's `values.yaml` defines `resources: { requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi } }` and `values-prod.yaml` only overrides `resources.requests.memory: 512Mi`, the merged value keeps `cpu: 100m` from the default and changes only `memory`. An environment-specific values file can therefore stay small, listing only what differs. (Lists are the exception: a list in an override replaces the default list entirely rather than merging.)

Before running `helm install` or `helm upgrade` against a real cluster, `helm template ./my-app -f values-prod.yaml` renders the same output locally, with no cluster interaction, printing the final YAML that would be sent to the API server. You can read it, diff it against a previous render, or pipe it into `kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f -` for an extra validation pass. `helm lint ./my-app` runs a separate set of structural checks (YAML that won't parse, malformed chart metadata, template errors) and is the first thing to run after editing a template, since it catches a large class of mistakes before you get to rendering. `helm upgrade --dry-run --debug` goes one step further and shows the rendered manifests as Helm would submit them.

sections.heading: The Multi-Line Indentation Trap
sections.body:
One templating mistake shows up constantly, because it looks correct until you render it: embedding a multi-line value (a resources block, a map of annotations, a whole config file's contents) with `toYaml` without accounting for indentation.

```yaml
# BROKEN: toYaml's own indentation doesn't match its surrounding context
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          resources:
{{ toYaml .Values.resources }}
```

`toYaml` serializes `.Values.resources` starting at column 0, with no awareness of how deeply nested it needs to sit inside the surrounding `containers:` block. The raw substitution above produces a `resources:` key followed by content at column 0, which doesn't nest under the container list item. The fix is `nindent`, which does two things at once: it inserts a newline before the content, and indents every line of that content by the given number of spaces:

```yaml
# FIXED
        - name: app
          resources:
{{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }}
```

`nindent 12` places the rendered block at 12 spaces of indentation: the `resources:` key sits at 10 spaces (under `- name:`, whose `name` key starts at 10), so its children belong 2 spaces further in. Getting this number wrong by one level produces YAML that is valid but wrong (the block attaches to the wrong parent key) or outright invalid, which is why you should run `helm template` and read its output after touching any template that embeds a nested structure this way. The bug is invisible in the template source and only appears in the rendered result.

examples.title: A Minimal Chart: values.yaml and a Parameterized Deployment
examples.code:
# values.yaml
replicaCount: 2
image:
  repository: my-registry/my-app
  tag: "1.4.0"
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 128Mi

---
# templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: {{ .Release.Name }}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: {{ .Release.Name }}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
          resources:
{{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }}
examples.explanation: Every field that could differ per environment or release (the replica count, the image tag, the resource requests) comes from `.Values` instead of being hardcoded. `{{ .Release.Name }}` is used for both the Deployment's name and the Pod template's label, so installing this chart twice under different release names (say `web-blue` and `web-green`) produces two non-colliding, independently selectable sets of objects with no change to the template. Running `helm template ./my-app` with no overrides renders this structure with `replicas: 2`, `image: "my-registry/my-app:1.4.0"`, and the resources block correctly nested. That rendered output is ordinary Kubernetes YAML by the time it reaches the API server; nothing template-specific survives.

examples.title: Overriding Values at Install Time
examples.code:
# Render with only the chart's own defaults (no overrides)
helm template web ./my-app | grep replicas
#   replicas: 2

# Render with a production values file plus a one-off --set override
helm template web ./my-app -f values-prod.yaml --set replicaCount=5 | grep replicas
#   replicas: 5

# values-prod.yaml itself only sets:
# replicaCount: 3
# image:
#   tag: "1.4.0-prod"
examples.explanation: Even though `values-prod.yaml` sets `replicaCount: 3`, the rendered output shows `replicas: 5`, because `--set` sits above `-f` files in Helm's precedence order, whatever order the flags appear in on the command line. CI/CD pipelines rely on this: a values file in the chart's repo captures the stable, reviewed configuration for an environment, while a `--set` flag on top handles a one-off override (a hotfix image tag, a temporary scale-up) without editing and committing a file first. `helm template` never touches a cluster; it's a local rendering step, which makes it the right tool for checking precedence like this before running `install` or `upgrade` for real.

examples.title: The nindent Bug, Broken and Fixed
examples.code:
# BROKEN: toYaml's output isn't indented to match its context
containers:
  - name: app
    resources:
{{ toYaml .Values.resources }}
# Renders to:
# containers:
#   - name: app
#     resources:
# requests:
#   cpu: 100m
#   memory: 128Mi
# Note: "requests" is at column 0, no longer nested under "resources" at all

# FIXED
containers:
  - name: app
    resources:
{{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 6 }}
# Renders to:
# containers:
#   - name: app
#     resources:
#       requests:
#         cpu: 100m
#         memory: 128Mi
examples.explanation: In the broken version, `toYaml` serializes the `resources` map starting at column 0 because it doesn't know it's being embedded several spaces deep; the raw `{{ toYaml ... }}` substitution drops that text in verbatim, indentation and all. The result still parses as YAML, but `requests` ends up as a top-level key instead of a child of `resources`, a structurally wrong render rather than a syntax error. That kind of bug survives a casual glance and only shows up when you diff the rendered output or watch the applied object misbehave. `nindent 6` fixes it by prefixing every line of the serialized block with 6 spaces (and a leading newline), nesting it under `resources:` at the depth this template position needs. Nothing tells you the right number to pass except counting the indentation of the surrounding YAML by hand, which is why running `helm template` and reading the rendered output, rather than trusting the template source, is the reliable way to catch this class of mistake.

misconceptions.description: The values baked into a chart's own values.yaml are essentially fixed once the chart is written -- meaningfully changing behavior per environment requires forking or hand-editing the chart itself.
misconceptions.clarification: values.yaml only supplies the lowest-precedence defaults; it's designed to be overridden without touching the chart, via one or more -f/--values files layered on top (later files win over earlier ones) and --set flags on the command line (which win over every file). A well-authored chart is written once and reused unmodified across every environment, with only the values changing. Forking the chart to change a value defeats the purpose of separating the template from its configuration, and leaves you merging upstream changes by hand every time the chart is updated.

misconceptions.description: A file under templates/ that looks like valid, complete Kubernetes YAML (aside from the {{ }} placeholders) could be applied directly with kubectl apply -f, since the {{ }} bits are just extra annotations Kubernetes would ignore.
misconceptions.clarification: Files under templates/ are Go template source, not Kubernetes manifests: the {{ }} syntax means nothing to the Kubernetes API server. Applying such a file directly would send literal text like `{{ .Values.replicaCount }}` as the value of a field expecting an integer, and the API server would reject it as malformed. Only Helm's rendering step (run internally by helm install/upgrade, or explicitly via helm template) substitutes real values and produces valid YAML. Nothing under templates/ is meant to be read by anything but Helm's template engine first.
misconceptions.fact: Files under templates/ are Go template source, not Kubernetes manifests, and the {{ }} syntax has no meaning to the Kubernetes API server.

exercises.prompt: A chart's values.yaml sets `replicaCount: 2`. A team maintains `values-prod.yaml` with `replicaCount: 3`. Someone runs the command below during an incident to temporarily scale up. What replica count does the rendered Deployment actually have, and why?
hints: Three different sources define replicaCount here: the chart's own values.yaml, the -f file, and --set. List them out and think about which one Helm treats as authoritative when they conflict.
Precedence, from lowest to highest, is: the chart's own values.yaml, then -f files in the order given, then --set flags.
--set is specifically designed for exactly this situation -- a one-off override that should win over whatever a checked-in values file says, without needing to edit that file.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 10. --set sits at the highest precedence level, above any -f file and above the chart's own values.yaml, regardless of the order the flags appear on the command line, so replicaCount=10 wins over both replicaCount: 3 (values-prod.yaml) and replicaCount: 2 (the chart's default).
exercises.solutionExplanation: Helm resolves conflicting values by a fixed precedence order, independent of the order flags are typed: --set (and --set-string/--set-file) wins over any -f/--values file, which wins over the chart's bundled values.yaml. Here replicaCount is defined three times (2 in the chart's values.yaml, 3 in values-prod.yaml, 10 via --set), and since --set is the highest-precedence source, the rendered Deployment has replicas: 10. That's why --set is the standard tool for a temporary override during an incident: it doesn't require editing or committing a change to values-prod.yaml, and its effect is scoped to this one upgrade invocation. (The next upgrade without the flag goes back to the file's 3, unless the flag is repeated or --reuse-values is used.)

exercises.prompt: This template is meant to attach a variable-length set of annotations from values.yaml onto a Deployment, but `helm template` produces YAML where the annotations end up as siblings of `metadata` instead of nested underneath it. Find and fix the bug.
exercises.code:
# values.yaml
annotations:
  team: platform
  owner: sre

# templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}
  annotations:
{{ toYaml .Values.annotations }}
spec:
  replicas: 1
hints: toYaml serializes .Values.annotations starting at column 0 -- it has no awareness of how many spaces of indentation this specific spot in the template actually needs.
Compare the indentation of `annotations:` above the {{ }} line to the indentation `toYaml`'s raw output would need to land at to nest correctly underneath it.
There's a template function specifically built to indent every line of a multi-line block by a fixed number of spaces before inserting it.
exercises.solutionCode:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}
  annotations:
{{- toYaml .Values.annotations | nindent 4 }}
spec:
  replicas: 1
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original `{{ toYaml .Values.annotations }}` drops the serialized map in at column 0, so `team: platform` and `owner: sre` line up with `apiVersion`/`metadata`/`spec`, making them siblings of the Deployment's top-level keys instead of children of `annotations`. Piping through `nindent 4` indents every line of the block by 4 spaces (`annotations:` sits at 2 spaces, so its children go one 2-space step further) and inserts a leading newline so the first annotation doesn't end up on the same line as `annotations:`. The leading `{{-` also trims the whitespace before the tag, avoiding a stray blank line.

assessments.prompt: A chart's values.yaml sets `image.tag: "1.0"`. You run `helm install web ./my-app -f values-a.yaml --set image.tag=2.0`, where values-a.yaml sets `image.tag: "1.5"`. What image tag ends up in the rendered manifest?
options: 1.0, because the chart's own values.yaml is always treated as the final source of truth and overrides every other layer.
1.5, because -f files are applied last, after --set flags are evaluated.
Helm raises an error because the same key is defined in three different places.
2.0, because --set has the highest precedence, overriding both the -f file and the chart's own values.yaml.
assessments.explanation: Helm's value precedence, lowest to highest, is: the chart's bundled values.yaml, then -f/--values files (later files overriding earlier ones), then --set flags, which win wherever they appear on the command line. So image.tag=2.0 from --set overrides both image.tag: "1.5" from values-a.yaml and image.tag: "1.0" from the chart's default. The “1.0, because the chart's own values.yaml…” and “1.5, because -f files are applied last…” options both misstate the order (values.yaml is the lowest-precedence source, and -f files are overridden by --set, not the reverse). The “Helm raises an error because the same…” option is wrong: Helm is designed to let the same key be set in several layered sources, which is what the override mechanism is for.

assessments.prompt: A chart's Chart.yaml has `version: 2.3.0` and `appVersion: 1.4.0`. The chart author fixes a bug in a template (say, a missing label) without changing anything about the application image itself. Which field, if any, should change as a result?
options: version should be bumped (e.g., to 2.3.1), since it tracks how many times the chart's own packaging has changed; appVersion should stay at 1.4.0, since it tracks the version of the deployed application, which hasn't changed at all.
Both fields must always be incremented together in lockstep, since Helm enforces that version and appVersion stay synchronized.
appVersion should be bumped instead, since any change to the packaging is considered part of the application's own versioning by Helm.
Neither field needs to change -- Chart.yaml's version fields are purely decorative and have no bearing on chart behavior.
assessments.explanation: version and appVersion are independent: you can ship a packaging fix without the application changing, or vice versa. A template-only bug fix is that case: the chart's packaging changed, so version should move, while the deployed application is unchanged, so appVersion stays. The “Neither field needs to change -- Chart.yaml's…” option dismisses fields that communicate real information to chart consumers (for example in helm search and artifact repositories). The “appVersion should be bumped instead, since any…” option reverses which field tracks which concern. The “Both fields must always be incremented together…” option invents an enforcement rule Helm doesn't have; nothing requires the two numbers to move together.

assessments.prompt: A template wraps a resources block in `{{- if .Values.resources }} ... {{- end }}` rather than rendering it unconditionally. What problem does this conditional specifically guard against?
options: It's purely a stylistic convention with no effect on whether the rendered YAML is valid either way.
It prevents Helm from crashing outright the moment .Values.resources is referenced anywhere in the chart.

It avoids emitting a resources: key with no meaningful content when resources hasn't actually been set for a given install -- rendering it unconditionally regardless of whether the value exists could produce output that's semantically empty or syntactically invalid depending on what follows.
It causes Helm to automatically substitute a hardcoded default resources block whenever the condition evaluates to false.
assessments.explanation: The conditional gates the whole block on the value being present. If resources was never set and the block rendered anyway, `toYaml` would emit `null` or an empty block under a `resources:` key, which is at best noise and at worst breaks the structure that follows, depending on the surrounding template. The “It prevents Helm from crashing outright…” option overstates the effect: referencing an unset value doesn't crash Helm by itself. The “It causes Helm to automatically substitute…” option invents a substitution the conditional doesn't provide; the else-branch here is 'emit nothing.' The “It's purely a stylistic convention…” option understates the effect this conditional has on the rendered output.

assessments.prompt: What do the leading `{{-` and trailing `-}}` whitespace-trim markers actually do in a Go template, and why does this concept treat them as more than a cosmetic detail?
options: They raise this particular value's precedence above any --set flag supplied later on the command line.

They strip the newline and indentation immediately before/after the tag, preventing stray blank lines from accumulating around conditionals and loops; combined with indent helpers like nindent, they control where generated blocks start, which can decide whether the rendered YAML is valid, not merely how it looks.
They tell the template engine to treat the enclosed expression as a raw string literal instead of evaluating it.
They force the template engine to render the enclosed block as JSON instead of YAML.
assessments.explanation: The trim markers strip surrounding whitespace and newlines. That looks cosmetic, but combined with `nindent` and `toYaml` it decides where each generated block starts, and so whether the rendered file is the YAML you intended. The “They tell the template engine to treat…” option confuses trim markers with a different templating concept (literal-string escaping). The “They raise this particular value's precedence above…” option invents a link to Helm's values precedence; trim markers are purely about template whitespace. The “They force the template engine to render…” option is false; the trim markers have no bearing on output format.

assessments.prompt: A chart's values.yaml defines `resources: { requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi } }`. An override values file sets only `resources.requests.memory: 512Mi`. What does the merged, final value of `resources.requests` end up being?
options: { memory: 512Mi } -- specifying any key under requests in an override file replaces the entire requests map wholesale, discarding cpu entirely along with any other key the chart had set.
{ cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi } -- the override is ignored entirely because it only sets a nested key rather than the whole resources block.
{ cpu: 100m, memory: 512Mi } -- the deep merge replaces only the specific key the override sets, preserving cpu from the chart's default since the override never mentioned it.
Helm raises an error, since resources.requests is defined in two different sources and can't be automatically reconciled.
assessments.explanation: Value merging is a deep merge on maps, not a wholesale replacement: overriding only resources.requests.memory keeps cpu: 100m from the chart's default and changes only the key the override names. The “{ memory: 512Mi } -- specifying any…” option describes a shallow, wholesale-replace strategy, which Helm doesn't use for maps. The “Helm raises an error, since resources.requests…” option invents an error condition; layering overrides across sources is the purpose of the mechanism. The “{ cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }…” option wrongly claims nested overrides are ignored, when they're what an override file is for.

assessments.prompt: What is the specific difference between what `helm lint` checks and what `helm template` checks?
options: They're functionally identical; helm lint is simply an older, deprecated alias for helm template.
helm lint requires an active connection to a Kubernetes cluster to run, while helm template works entirely offline.
helm template only works after a chart has already been installed as a live release; helm lint is the only one of the two that works beforehand.

helm lint runs structural checks against the chart itself (missing required values, malformed chart metadata, YAML that won't parse) without necessarily needing to produce full rendered output; helm template actually renders the chart's templates into final YAML using the given values, letting you inspect exactly what would be sent to the API server.
assessments.explanation: The two commands have distinct roles: helm lint catches structural chart-authoring mistakes (unparseable YAML, malformed metadata, template errors) as a fast first check, while helm template performs the full rendering step and prints the output that would be applied, so you can read or diff it before it reaches a cluster. The “They're functionally identical; helm lint is simply…” option collapses two different commands into one. The “helm template only works after a chart…” option is backwards and wrong on the facts: neither command requires an existing release; both operate on a chart directory. The “helm lint requires an active connection…” option is false: neither needs a live cluster connection.

assessments.prompt: A teammate maintaining 15 microservices across 4 environments (dev/staging/prod/sandbox) asks why the team should adopt Helm instead of continuing to hand-maintain a separate YAML file per service per environment. Explain the core problem Helm's templating solves, and walk through what changes concretely for a single configuration change (like a new default resource limit) once the switch is made.
assessments.modelAnswer: With 15 services across 4 environments, the team maintains close to 60 YAML files that aren't independent in any meaningful sense: they're 60 near-copies of a much smaller number of patterns, differing in a handful of parameters like image tag, replica count, and resource limits. Plain YAML doesn't represent that relationship, so all 60 files have to be kept in sync by hand, and the failure mode is drift: a resource limit gets bumped in production during an incident and never makes it to staging, or a new required label lands in some files but not others because the editor didn't know to touch every copy. There's also no single artifact for 'this configuration as deployed to prod last week'; reconstructing what changed between two deploys means diffing raw files by hand. Helm's templating restructures this: instead of 60 independent files, the team writes one chart per service (15 charts) with Go-template manifests under templates/, plus a small values file per environment holding only the values that differ, often just image tag, replica count, and a few resource numbers, with everything else falling back to the chart's defaults. Rolling out a new default resource limit becomes a single edit to one chart's values.yaml (or one small values-prod.yaml for an environment-specific override) instead of four edits, one per environment, and any environment that hasn't overridden that value picks up the new default on its next helm upgrade, with no risk of forgetting one of the copies, because there are no separate copies.

concepts.title: Helm Releases: Install, Upgrade, and Rollback
concepts.description: A Helm release is a named, versioned instance of a chart running in a cluster. Every install and upgrade advances that instance's own revision history, and that tracked history, not anything in the Kubernetes API itself, is what makes helm rollback a fast, reliable way to undo a bad deploy without reconstructing anything by hand.
learningObjectives: Define what a Helm 'release' is and distinguish it clearly from a 'chart' -- a template versus a specific deployed instance of it.
Use helm install, helm upgrade, helm history, and helm rollback, and describe what each one does to a release's revision history.
Explain where Helm 3 stores release state by default (a Secret per revision) and why that matters for RBAC and cluster inspection.
Explain what --atomic and helm upgrade --install accomplish, and why both matter for CI/CD safety.
Predict what happens if a chart's rendered manifests fail to apply cleanly partway through an upgrade, with and without --atomic.
Explain why uninstalling and reinstalling a release is not equivalent to upgrading it, and what capability is lost by doing so.

sections.heading: A Release Is Not the Same Thing as a Chart
sections.body:
A **chart** is a template: a directory of Go-template manifests plus a values.yaml, portable and reusable, with no relationship yet to any running cluster. A **release** is what you get when you run `helm install <release-name> <chart>` against a cluster: a named, running instance of that chart, with a specific set of resolved values, in a specific namespace, carrying its own revision history from then on. `helm list` (add `-A` for all namespaces) shows the releases in a cluster with their current revision and status.

The same chart can back multiple independent releases at once. Installing `my-app` twice, as `helm install team-a-web ./my-app -f team-a-values.yaml` and `helm install team-b-web ./my-app -f team-b-values.yaml`, produces two releases, `team-a-web` and `team-b-web`, each with its own revision history, installed values, and live Kubernetes objects (distinguished by the templated `{{ .Release.Name }}` in their names, as in the previous concept's example). Upgrading or rolling back one has no effect on the other. They share only the chart they were installed from, the way two houses built from one blueprint share nothing structurally once built.

A Deployment object has its own rollout history (tracked via ReplicaSets, covered in Deployments, ReplicaSets, and Rolling Updates). A Helm release's revision history is a *separate, higher-level* concept: it versions the *entire rendered set of manifests* a chart produces (a Deployment, a Service, a ConfigMap, and more, all at once), not any single object's history. Rolling back a Helm release can therefore revert several objects' worth of changes in one operation, which a single Deployment's rollout history can't express.

sections.heading: Install, Upgrade, Rollback: The Lifecycle Commands
sections.body:
`helm install web ./my-app -f values-prod.yaml` renders the chart with the merged values and applies the result, creating the release `web` at **revision 1**. `helm upgrade web ./my-app -f values-prod.yaml` re-renders the chart (picking up changes to the templates, to values-prod.yaml, or to any --set flags supplied again), computes what needs to change against the live objects, applies it, and advances the release to **revision 2**. Every later `helm upgrade` (a new image tag, a scaled replica count, a config change) creates another revision: 3, 4, 5, and so on, each retaining its rendered manifests and resolved values.

`helm history web` lists every revision with its status (deployed, superseded, failed) and a short description. `helm rollback web 2` reverts the *live* objects to match revision 2's stored manifests, but it creates a **new** revision (say revision 6, if the release was at 5) whose *content* matches revision 2, instead of rewinding the counter to 2. The revision number only goes up; think of `helm rollback` as 'create a new revision using old content,' not 'travel back in time.' Running `helm rollback web` with no revision number rolls back to the previous revision.

```bash
helm install web ./my-app -f values-prod.yaml     # revision 1
helm upgrade web ./my-app --set image.tag=1.5.0    # revision 2
helm upgrade web ./my-app --set image.tag=1.6.0    # revision 3 (bad release)
helm rollback web 2                                # revision 4, content == revision 2
helm history web
# REVISION  STATUS      CHART           APP VERSION  DESCRIPTION
# 1         superseded  my-app-0.1.0    1.4.0        Install complete
# 2         superseded  my-app-0.1.0    1.5.0        Upgrade complete
# 3         superseded  my-app-0.1.0    1.6.0        Upgrade complete
# 4         deployed    my-app-0.1.0    1.5.0        Rollback to 2
```

sections.heading: Where Release State Lives
sections.body:
By default, Helm 3 records each release revision as a **Secret** in the release's own namespace, conventionally named `sh.helm.release.v1.<release-name>.v<revision>`: one Secret per revision, holding the rendered manifests and resolved values (compressed and base64-encoded). `kubectl get secrets -n <namespace> -l owner=helm` lists them, and two consequences are worth internalizing.

First, because it's a Secret (not a ConfigMap), the facts from the ConfigMaps and Secrets concept apply: the content is base64-encoded, not encrypted, and the RBAC controlling who can read Secrets in a namespace also controls who can read Helm's release history and resolved values there, including anything sensitive passed via `--set` or a values file. (It's one reason to avoid putting real credentials on the command line, where they also land in shell history.) You can read back what a release was installed with using `helm get values web` and `helm get manifest web`. A user who can't read Secrets in a namespace will find `helm history` and `helm get values` failing against it, even if they can see the Deployments and Services the release created.

Second, these revision Secrets accumulate as a release keeps being upgraded. `--history-max` (settable per install/upgrade, default 10) caps how many revisions Helm retains before pruning the oldest. Retaining fewer saves a little etcd storage but limits how far back `helm rollback` can reach, since a pruned revision's manifests are gone.

sections.heading: Atomic Upgrades and CI/CD Safety
sections.body:
By default, if a `helm upgrade` applies its rendered manifests but a resulting object then fails to become healthy (a new Pod template that never passes readiness, a rollout that stalls), Helm doesn't notice or react. The release can be left with new objects created but the rollout unfinished, and nothing restores the previous good state; a human has to notice and run `helm rollback`.

`--atomic` changes this: it makes Helm wait for the upgrade's resources to become ready (implying `--wait`) and, if that doesn't happen within the timeout, automatically roll back to the release's previous successful revision. That is the property a CI/CD pipeline needs, because it turns 'a bad deploy leaves the cluster half-upgraded and degraded until someone notices' into 'a bad deploy reverts to the last known-good revision within the pipeline's own deploy step, and the pipeline fails loudly if that revert itself fails.'

```bash
helm upgrade web ./my-app --set image.tag=broken-tag --atomic --timeout 5m
# Error: UPGRADE FAILED: release web failed, and has been rolled back due to atomic being set: <timeout reason>
```

Separately, `helm upgrade --install` (often `upgrade -i`) is the idiomatic deploy command for a CI pipeline because the pipeline doesn't need to branch on whether the release exists yet: it upgrades the release if it's installed and does a first-time install if it isn't, so one command covers the first deploy and every deploy after it. Add `--create-namespace` if the target namespace may not exist yet, and `--wait` if you want the command to block until the resources are ready (`--atomic` already implies it).

sections.heading: Why Reinstalling Is Not the Same as Upgrading
sections.body:
When an upgrade seems stuck or confusing, it's tempting to `helm uninstall web` and then `helm install web ./my-app` fresh. The application ends up running again, but you lose something: the entire revision history from every earlier install and upgrade, and with it the ability to `helm rollback` to any of those states, because uninstalling deletes the release's tracked Secrets, not just the live application objects. (`helm uninstall --keep-history` retains them, but a plain uninstall doesn't.)

There's also an availability cost: uninstall-then-install deletes everything and then creates everything fresh, with a gap where none of the release's objects exist, similar to the `Recreate` strategy's outage window from earlier. A normal `helm upgrade` instead drives an ordinary Kubernetes rolling update (assuming the Deployment uses `RollingUpdate`), a gradual, overlapping transition. Reserve reinstalling for genuinely broken situations, such as a release stuck in a state no upgrade or rollback can recover, not as a routine alternative to `helm upgrade` for shipping a change.

examples.title: A Full Install-Upgrade-Rollback Cycle
examples.code:
helm install web ./my-app --set image.tag=1.0.0
# NAME: web
# LAST DEPLOYED: ...
# STATUS: deployed
# REVISION: 1

helm upgrade web ./my-app --set image.tag=1.1.0
# REVISION: 2

helm history web
# REVISION  STATUS      APP VERSION  DESCRIPTION
# 1         superseded  1.0.0        Install complete
# 2         deployed    1.1.0        Upgrade complete

helm rollback web 1
# Rollback was a success! Happy Helming!

helm history web
# REVISION  STATUS      APP VERSION  DESCRIPTION
# 1         superseded  1.0.0        Install complete
# 2         superseded  1.1.0        Upgrade complete
# 3         deployed    1.0.0        Rollback to 1
examples.explanation: Look at the final `helm history`: no revision was deleted or rewound. Revision 3 is a new entry whose content matches revision 1's (image tag 1.0.0), and revision 3, not revision 1, now has STATUS: deployed. That shows helm rollback always moves the revision counter forward; 'rolling back' describes the effect on the live objects' content, not a reversal of the release's version number. A second `helm rollback web 2` from here would create revision 4 with image tag 1.1.0's content, and so on: the history only grows.

examples.title: Inspecting Release State as Secrets
examples.code:
kubectl get secrets -n default -l owner=helm
# NAME                          TYPE                 AGE
# sh.helm.release.v1.web.v1     helm.sh/release.v1   14m
# sh.helm.release.v1.web.v2     helm.sh/release.v1   9m
# sh.helm.release.v1.web.v3     helm.sh/release.v1   1m

kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n default --as=system:serviceaccount:default:ci-deployer
# no

helm history web --namespace default
# Error: query: failed to query with labels: secrets is forbidden: User "system:serviceaccount:default:ci-deployer" cannot list resource "secrets" in API group "" in the namespace "default"
# (the ci-deployer identity can't read the release Secrets, so Helm can't see the history)
examples.explanation: Each revision from the previous example produced its own Secret, with the release name and revision number in its name, which is the storage mechanism described in this concept. The second block shows the RBAC consequence: a ServiceAccount denied access to Secrets in this namespace can't read Helm's release history either, even if it has full permission on the Deployments and Services the release created, because Helm's bookkeeping is a Secret, subject to the same access control as any other Secret in the namespace.

examples.title: --atomic Catching a Broken Upgrade
examples.code:
# Without --atomic: a broken upgrade is applied and left half-done
helm upgrade web ./my-app --set image.tag=typo-tag
# Release "web" has been upgraded. Happy Helming!
# (but the new Pods are stuck in ImagePullBackOff; nobody has rolled anything back)

kubectl get pods -l app=web
# web-8a1e2f4c3-h9z1x   0/1   ImagePullBackOff

# With --atomic: the same broken upgrade self-heals
helm upgrade web ./my-app --set image.tag=typo-tag --atomic --timeout 3m
# Error: UPGRADE FAILED: release web failed, and has been rolled back due to atomic being set: timed out waiting for the condition

helm history web
# (current revision's content still matches the last GOOD image tag, unaffected by the failed attempt)
examples.explanation: Without --atomic, `helm upgrade` reports success as soon as it finishes applying the rendered manifests; it doesn't wait to confirm the new Pods become healthy, so a broken image tag can leave the cluster half-upgraded (some old Pods possibly already scaled down, new Pods stuck) with no automatic correction. With --atomic, Helm waits for readiness up to --timeout and, on failure, rolls back to the previous good revision itself, using the same mechanism as a manual `helm rollback`, triggered automatically. That's why CI/CD pipelines deploying via Helm should include --atomic on every upgrade instead of treating it as optional.

misconceptions.description: helm rollback web 2 restores revision 2 as the current revision, so the release's revision counter goes back down to 2 and the next upgrade after that would become revision 3.
misconceptions.clarification: The revision counter only goes up. Rolling back to revision 2 from a release at revision 5 creates a new revision 6 whose rendered manifests and values match revision 2's. It doesn't delete revisions 3, 4, or 5, and it doesn't make revision 2 current again. The next upgrade after the rollback would be revision 7, not 3. helm history after any rollback shows every revision that ever existed, including the rollback as a new entry, never a shortened or rewound list.

misconceptions.description: Once a release is installed, the chart's source directory (or its entry in a local/remote chart repository) needs to stay available, since Kubernetes has to keep referring back to it to keep the release's objects running.
misconceptions.clarification: Once helm install or upgrade has applied the rendered manifests, the resulting Kubernetes objects (Deployments, Services, and so on) are ordinary, independent objects in etcd, and nothing about their operation depends on the chart's source files existing anywhere, any more than a Deployment applied from deployment.yaml depends on that file staying on disk. The chart's source is needed again only for the next upgrade; rollback and uninstall work from Helm's own stored copy of each revision's manifests, in the release's revision Secrets.

exercises.prompt: A release goes through: install (rev 1, tag=1.0), upgrade (rev 2, tag=1.1), upgrade (rev 3, tag=1.2), then `helm rollback web 1`. What revision number is now marked 'deployed', and what image tag do the live Pods actually run?
exercises.code:
helm install web ./my-app --set image.tag=1.0
helm upgrade web ./my-app --set image.tag=1.1
helm upgrade web ./my-app --set image.tag=1.2
helm rollback web 1
helm history web   # ?
hints: Rolling back doesn't erase or reuse an old revision number -- it always creates a new one on top of whatever the release is currently at.
The release was at revision 3 right before the rollback command ran. What's the next available revision number after 3?
The NEW revision's CONTENT (image tag) comes from whichever old revision you rolled back to -- track those two things (revision number vs. content) separately.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Revision 4 is now marked 'deployed', and the live Pods run image tag 1.0: the content of revision 1, copied forward into a brand-new revision 4, rather than revision 1 itself becoming current again.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Before the rollback, the release has three revisions: 1 (tag 1.0), 2 (tag 1.1), 3 (tag 1.2, currently deployed). helm rollback web 1 doesn't resurrect revision 1 or delete revisions 2 and 3. It creates a new revision, 4, whose manifests and values are copied from revision 1's stored state, and marks revision 4 as deployed. The answer has two independent parts: the revision NUMBER now current is 4 (the counter only climbs), while the running CONTENT (image tag 1.0) matches revision 1's. A later helm history web would show four entries: 1, 2, 3 superseded and 4 deployed, with a description like 'Rollback to 1'.

exercises.prompt: This CI deploy script fails every run after the very first one, with 'Error: INSTALLATION FAILED: cannot re-use a name that is still in use.' The team wants every merge to main to deploy the latest image, whether or not this is the first deploy ever. Find and fix the bug.
hints: helm install has no notion of 'update if it already exists' -- what verb does Helm provide specifically for a release that might already be installed?
There's a single Helm command that installs a release if it doesn't exist yet, or upgrades it if it does, without the script needing to check which case it's in.
The fix is a one-word change to the command being run, not a change to any of the flags.
exercises.solutionExplanation: helm install is a one-time operation: calling it again for an existing release name fails with the error shown, like kubectl create against an existing object. helm upgrade --install (the --install flag, often abbreviated -i) is built for repeated deploys from CI: it upgrades the release if web exists, or does a first-time install if it doesn't, so the same command works on the first deploy and every deploy after it, with no branching in the script. Adding --atomic --timeout 5m (not required to fix the reported error, but a worthwhile CI/CD safety improvement from this concept) also makes a broken image tag revert to the previous good revision automatically instead of leaving a half-upgraded release in place.

assessments.prompt: By default, where does Helm 3 store the rendered manifests and resolved values for each release revision?
options: In a Secret object per revision, in the release's own namespace, subject to the same RBAC rules as any other Secret.
In a dedicated Tiller server component running inside the cluster.
Only locally, in a hidden directory on the machine that ran the helm command.
In a ConfigMap per release, shared across all of that release's revisions.
assessments.explanation: Helm 3 stores each revision's rendered manifests and values as a Secret (named sh.helm.release.v1.<release>.v<revision>) in the release's namespace: one Secret per revision, not per release, governed by ordinary Kubernetes RBAC like any other Secret. The “In a dedicated Tiller server component running…” option describes Helm 2's architecture; Helm 3 removed Tiller and talks to the Kubernetes API using the user's own credentials. The “Only locally, in a hidden directory…” option is false: state lives in the cluster so that helm history and rollback work from any machine with cluster access. The “In a ConfigMap per release, shared across…” option is wrong on both counts: it's a Secret, not a ConfigMap, and there's one per revision.

assessments.prompt: The same chart `my-app` is installed twice: once as release `team-a-web` and once as release `team-b-web`, each with its own values file. `team-a-web` is then rolled back to an earlier revision. What happens to `team-b-web` as a result?
options: Helm refuses to roll back team-a-web at all unless team-b-web is rolled back in the same operation.
Nothing happens to team-b-web at all -- each release has its own independent revision history and its own live objects.
team-b-web is also rolled back automatically, since both releases share the same underlying chart and Helm keeps sibling releases derived from it synchronized.
team-b-web's own revision counter resets to 1, since rolling back any release derived from a shared chart resets version tracking cluster-wide.
assessments.explanation: Upgrading or rolling back one release has no effect on another; they share only the chart they were installed from, the way two houses built from one blueprint share nothing structurally once built. Each release's revision history, live objects, and current values are independent bookkeeping keyed by release name. The “team-b-web is also rolled back automatically, since…”, “team-b-web's own revision counter resets to 1…”, and “Helm refuses to roll back team-a-web…” options all invent a cross-release coupling that Helm doesn't have; releases are isolated from one another even when derived from the same chart.

assessments.prompt: A chart's templates include a Deployment, a Service, and a ConfigMap. After several `helm upgrade` calls, the team runs `helm rollback web 2`. How does this differ from running `kubectl rollout undo deployment/web` directly?
options: helm rollback reverts the entire rendered set of objects the chart produces -- the Deployment, the Service, and the ConfigMap together, as one unit -- based on the release's own higher-level revision history, whereas kubectl rollout undo only reverts that one specific Deployment's own rollout history, with no awareness of the Service or ConfigMap at all.
They're functionally identical -- helm rollback simply calls kubectl rollout undo internally on every Deployment in the chart, and does nothing else.
kubectl rollout undo actually reverts more objects overall than helm rollback, since it acts directly on the cluster rather than going through Helm's abstraction layer.
Neither command is capable of acting on more than one object per invocation; both require being run separately against each object in the chart.
assessments.explanation: A Helm release's revision history is a separate, higher-level concept: it versions the entire rendered set of manifests a chart produces, not any single object's history, while a Deployment's own rollout history covers only that one object. Rolling back a release can therefore revert several objects in one operation, which a single Deployment's rollout history can't express. (Helm applies the objects one after another, so this is one command, not a transaction across the cluster.) The “They're functionally identical -- helm rollback simply…” option understates what helm rollback reverts. The “kubectl rollout undo actually reverts more objects…” option reverses which mechanism has the broader scope. The “Neither command is capable of acting…” option is false for helm rollback, which acts on multiple objects in one command.

assessments.prompt: A release has been upgraded 15 times under the default `--history-max` setting of 10. Can `helm rollback web 2` still succeed?
options: No -- rollback is only ever possible to the single immediately preceding revision, regardless of what history-max is set to.
Yes, because Helm always guarantees revision 1 and every subsequent even-numbered revision are retained regardless of history-max.
Yes, always -- history-max only limits how many revisions helm history displays on screen; it never actually deletes any revision's underlying stored data.
Not necessarily -- history-max caps how many old revisions Helm actually retains before pruning the oldest ones.
assessments.explanation: Revision Secrets accumulate as a release is upgraded, and `--history-max` caps how many old revisions Helm retains before pruning the oldest, so retaining fewer limits how far back helm rollback can reach, since a pruned revision's manifests are gone. After 15 upgrades there are 16 revisions, and with a cap of 10 only the latest 10 remain, so revision 2 has already been pruned and that rollback target is unavailable. The “Yes, always -- history-max only limits how…” option misdescribes history-max as a display limit instead of a retention policy. The “Yes, because Helm always guarantees revision 1…” option invents an even/odd retention guarantee. The “No -- rollback is only ever possible…” option is false: helm rollback can target any retained revision, not just the immediately preceding one.

assessments.prompt: A CI pipeline's very first deploy of a brand-new release runs `helm upgrade web ./my-app -f values-prod.yaml` (without the --install flag). What happens?
options: It succeeds and performs a first-time install automatically, since helm upgrade silently falls back to install behavior whenever no prior release exists.
It succeeds, but creates the release starting at revision number 0 instead of 1, to signal that it took the upgrade code path.
It fails, because there is no existing release named web yet for helm upgrade to act on -- helm upgrade expects a release to already exist.
It always succeeds identically to helm install, since upgrade and install have been fully interchangeable commands since Helm 3.
assessments.explanation: helm upgrade on its own has no fallback for a nonexistent release; it acts on a release that's already installed (you'd see an error like `"web" has no deployed releases`). helm upgrade --install exists to remove the need for a pipeline to branch on 'does this release exist yet,' which only makes sense if plain helm upgrade doesn't handle that case. The “It succeeds and performs a first-time install…” option invents the fallback that --install adds. The “It succeeds, but creates the release starting…” option invents a nonstandard revision-numbering behavior. The “It always succeeds identically to helm install…” option is false: if upgrade and install were interchangeable, --install wouldn't need to exist as a separate flag.

assessments.prompt: A team decides that instead of debugging a confusing `helm upgrade`, they'll just run `helm uninstall web` followed by `helm install web ./my-app`. Besides the brief availability gap, what specific capability do they lose by doing this instead of fixing the upgrade?
options: The application's persistent data is always deleted as a direct, guaranteed consequence of running helm uninstall, regardless of what storage mechanism backs it.
The entire revision history built up by every prior install and upgrade.
Nothing meaningful -- uninstalling and reinstalling preserves the release's revision history internally, so helm rollback to any earlier revision still works afterward.
Only the single most recent revision is lost; every earlier revision remains rollback-able after the reinstall completes.
assessments.explanation: Uninstalling deletes the release's tracked Secrets along with the live objects, so the entire revision history, and the ability to roll back to any earlier state, is gone, and the fresh install starts over at revision 1. The “Nothing meaningful -- uninstalling and reinstalling preserves…” option claims the opposite. The “Only the single most recent revision…” option understates the loss, which is total. The “The application's persistent data is always deleted…” option overclaims guaranteed data deletion; whether persistent data survives depends on separate mechanisms (like a PVC's reclaim policy from the Storage module), not on helm uninstall universally destroying it.

assessments.prompt: Explain what --atomic changes about how helm upgrade handles a broken deploy, and why a CI/CD pipeline that deploys via Helm should treat it as close to mandatory rather than optional.
assessments.modelAnswer: Without --atomic, helm upgrade's job ends once it has applied the newly rendered manifests to the cluster; it doesn't wait to confirm the resulting objects become healthy. So a broken change (a bad image tag, a misconfigured probe, anything that stops the new Pods ever becoming Ready) can be 'successfully' applied by Helm's accounting while the cluster is left degraded and half-upgraded: possibly some old Pods already scaled down, new Pods stuck failing to start, and nothing correcting it until a human notices and runs helm rollback. --atomic changes this contract: helm upgrade implicitly waits (as with --wait) for the upgraded resources to reach a healthy state within --timeout, and if they don't, it rolls back to the release's previous successful revision on its own, then reports a clear failure instead of a false success. For a CI/CD pipeline this is the difference between 'a bad deploy degrades production until someone happens to notice, minutes or hours later' and 'a bad deploy is caught and reverted within the pipeline's deploy step, and the build goes red immediately, where the mistake was introduced.' Since automated deployment assumes changes ship without a human watching each one, --atomic supplies the safety net an operator would otherwise provide by hand, which is why it's close to mandatory rather than a nice-to-have flag.
